name: Davis Divan
hook: In 1947 a Los Angeles used-car salesman promised America a four-seat family car with three wheels, and it nearly worked.
story: Picture Los Angeles in November 1947. The war is over, and everyone wants a new car. At the Ambassador Hotel, a used-car salesman named Gary Davis pulls the cover off his answer. It has three wheels. One in front, two behind. The body is aluminium and smooth as an aeroplane. The headlights hide away. Four people sit side by side on one wide bench. Davis says it will do 100 miles an hour and cost just $995. He loves to show off the turning circle. With Davis at the wheel, the little prototype swings round in about thirteen feet at 50 miles an hour, and it stays on its feet. But selling a dream is easier than building one. Only a handful of cars are finished, somewhere between thirteen and seventeen, before the company falls apart. Davis is convicted of fraud and grand theft and serves about two years. That should be the end of it. Instead, the few survivors became treasures, and today museums show them off.
description: The Davis Divan is a three-wheeled, four-seat car built in California by the Davis Motorcar Company from 1947 to 1949. Gary Davis based it on the Californian, a one-off three-wheeled roadster Frank Kurtis built in 1941 for Joel Thorne. It has an aluminium body on a steel frame, a single bench seat, hideaway headlights and built-in hydraulic jacks. A Hercules four-cylinder engine drives the rear wheels through a three-speed manual gearbox. Only a handful were made before the company failed.
